subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPEAL TO PROVINCIAL COURT OF APPEAL IN DIVORCE AND MATRIMONIAL CAUSES

speechtext: Mr. H. C. GREEN (Vancouver South) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 15, to provide for appeal to the court of appeal of the province of British Columbia in divorce and matrimonial causes.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPEAL TO PROVINCIAL COURT OF APPEAL IN DIVORCE AND MATRIMONIAL CAUSES
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPEAL TO PROVINCIAL COURT OF APPEAL IN DIVORCE AND MATRIMONIAL CAUSES
speechtext:
In the province of British Columbia the supreme court, which is the trial court of the province, has been trying divorce cases for many years. Its right to do so is based on the law of England, as of the year 1858, which has been held to have been in force in British Columbia when that province came into confederation. But it has been held also that the court of appeal for the province of British Columbia has no jurisdiction to hear appeals in divorce matters. The result is that the only appeal is to the privy council, and that means, of course, that there is no appeal at all except for the very wealthy people of the province. In every other province of the dominion in which the courts have and exercise jurisdiction in divorce causes there is an appeal to the appellate court of the particular province. This national parliament alone has the power to correct this situation, because by the British North America Act we were given the exclusive legislative authority in divorce matters. The purpose of this bill is merely to bring the practice in British Columbia into line with the practice in the other provinces.
31111-37J

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPEAL TO PROVINCIAL COURT OF APPEAL IN DIVORCE AND MATRIMONIAL CAUSES
speechtext: Is the power of the various provinces by statute or otherwise?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPEAL TO PROVINCIAL COURT OF APPEAL IN DIVORCE AND MATRIMONIAL CAUSES
speechtext:
This parliament passed a statute six or seven years ago giving the courts of Ontario power to grant divorces, which I believe has been taken to include the power to hear appeals. Our difficulty in British Columbia arises by reason of legal decisions. It may be that these decisions are wrong, but they come from courts as high as the Supreme Court of Canada; and our present position is this, that there is really no appeal in this serious matter of divorce. The bill aims to set that position right.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speechtext: From a practical standpoint I agree entirely with the view taken by the leader of the opposition. Of course, I cannot offer a legal opinion except that of the Department of Justice, but looking at the matter as a practical one it is quite possible for a default by an individual debtor to occur while the lending institution is still lending to new borrowers.

subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext: Quite so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext:
Let us assume for the moment that the plan continues in operation for a year. It is conceivable that some of the earlier borrowers at the end of the year may be in default, but at the same time the lending institution is continuing to lend to new borrowers. The manner in which the guarantee shall become effective as between the lending institution and the government has not yet been worked out in detail because of that difficulty. We have endeavoured to leave it subject to future arrangement, but it is important, as the leader of the opposition says, that whatever is done should have sound law behind it. The Department of Justice has said, regarding the matter, that once the debtor has made default the liability of the guarantor arises in the absence of provisions to the contrary in the agreement. The creditor is not bound to request the debtor to pay or to sue the debtor before proceeding against the guarantor. The guarantor, however, cannot be permitted to suffer by reason of any arrangement which has taken place between the creditor and the debtor. The rule is that any material alteration in the terms of the debt which is guaranteed, made by the creditor and the debtor without the guarantor's assent, will discharge the guarantor, and a binding agreement by the creditor to give the debtor an extension of time is deemed to be a material alteration. That is precisely the point my right hon. friend makes. It is important however to observe that the guarantor is not discharged if he agreed in the contract of guarantee or in some other way that time might be given to the debtor with impunity or if he afterwards confirmed any agreement giving time. Mere omission on the part of the creditor to press the debtor for payment will not, if there is no binding agreement to give time, discharge the guarantor even if the debtor subsequently becomes insolvent. By a binding agreement is meant an agreement given for valuable consideration and enforceable by debtor and creditor. The intention is to execute a contract of guarantee with each lending institution. The contract will be made subject to the act and the

Home Improvement Loans
regulations made under the act, and the regulations will contain the conditions upon which an extension of time will be granted. Thus the lending institutions will have in the contract of guarantee itself the consent of the government to extensions of time, subject to certain conditions.
The question arises whether there is power under paragraphs (b) and (f) of clause 8 to make regulations permitting the lending institutions to grant extensions of time. The Department of Justice, while not admitting that the bill as now drafted is defective in this respect, thought that as the point had been raised it would be wiser to insert a new paragraph (c) in section 8 to remove all doubt. Perhaps I might read that now, although we have not yet reached the section. Paragraph (c) as amended would read as follows:
In the event of actual or pending default by a borrower the extent to which the lending institution and the borrower may, notwithstanding the provisions of paragraph (c) of section 6 of this act, alter or revise any of the terms of their agreement respecting a home improvement loan without discharging the guarantee under this act.
With this amendment the Department of Justice say that regulations could be passed under which the lending institutions would be able to grant extensions of time in certain cases even if some of the instalments were not payable until more than three or five years, as the case may be, after the loan was first made. That is the advice I have on that point.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
That question raises one of the difficulties of trying to qualify the term "owner" in connection with legislation of this kind which does not involve any security being taken on the property by the lender. My hon. friend will understand that if we limited "owner" to the literal meaning of the term "ownership" it would debar a great many people in various sections of the country where the long term lease method of holding property is in force. From the point of view of the present measure it is practically effectual ownership that is meant. At any rate such a long term lease certainly should not disqualify a person occupying a dwelling from what we intend to accomplish. That is why the words "long term lease" have been used. As a matter of fact we are thinking of widening it a little more; we are proposing to add the term "life tenants," because from the point of view of this legislation a life tenant ought to have just as much right to go to the bank and get a loan with which to improve the property of which he is the tenant. Then, in order to be sure that we are not debarring any class of person who ought to qualify, we are proposing to add at the end of (i) the words "and any persons having rights approximating ownership." This question arose in a case involving what in the west we used to call squatter's rights. The person concerned had occupied his dwelling for a long time. There was no title other than that which might obtain under

subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS

Far be it from me to say anything in behalf of the lending institutions; they will be quite capable of looking after themselves in making the agreements. But the lending institutions will not be willing to wait for eight or ten months more at a discount rate of 3i per cent. They will desire to be reimbursed as far as possible, at least to lhe extent of fifteen per cent of their loan, or to follow the course of collecting from their debtor, unless we do something to mark the beginning of the obligation to pay.

I do not see how we can get along with this loose-and I must call it an extremely loose -way of expressing it. I do not wish to be critical, but I believe the minister made it clear the other day that he was endeavouring to use terms general enough to permit of every case falling within it, because this is a measure not only to provide employment but to improve homes. I agree with that, but it seems to me that the terms cannot be so general as to leave them open on the one hand to abuse or on the other hand1 to fault finding on the part of the lending institution, which would place the unfortunate creditor in the position just now mentioned by the minister, namely that of being hounded to death. It seems to me the observations of the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) as to whether we should use the word "taken" or "required" would apply to the question of the taking of security, to which the minister has just referred. One means the act of the lending institution; it is a discretionary right. The other is a prohibition. That is the difference between the two. When we say "shall be required" we mean that they shall not ask him for security; but if he volunteers to give it, because of the general attitude of mind of the bank manager or the lending institution manager, that is the end of it- if he gives it. But if we say it "shall not be taken," then you have a positive enactment against it. On the other hand, the point the minister has just made, and concerning which he said he wished the opinion of the committee, is the one which arises there. We say they shall not take security, and they do not take security. There is default in the first payment, and then they say, " We want security for this loan, or we will sue."

speechtext: The minister has suggested that certain sections of the bill should be held in abeyance pending consideration by the Department of Justice of criticisms which might be offered in this discussion. be clearer phraseology than is here used. I am simply suggesting that the minister take the opinion of his legal advisers with regard to the matter before the bill finally passes committee.

No lending institution will be able at any time to receive a greater amount than is represented by fifteen per centum of the amount they have loaned under this plan. I intend that it shall be possible to deal with individual ascertained losses and to pay the guarantee once the government has ascertained that a loss has actually occurred with respect to a particular case.

aggregate paid of such losses cannot exceed fifteen per cent of the amount which that institution as a whole lent. That is the way in which we want it to work. If the draftsmen have not conveyed that meaning I am sorry.

speechtext:
I merely suggest, following the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling) that section 8(b) does not cover the exigency which the minister has stated. The section says that the governor in council may make regulations in regard to-
.	.	. the measures to be taken and the
procedure to be followed for the collection of the amount outstanding of the home improvement loan and the method of determining the amount of loss, if any.

I should like to know if
I have understood the minister aright. Take a case such as this. A lending institution lends to one hundred persons. Eighty-five per cent of them pay their loans in full; that leaves fifteen per cent. speechtext: My hon. friend is subdividing the matter into persons. I assume, if I caught the remarks-

There will be many thousands of loans made by the same lending institution, and there will be differing degrees of default. That is to say, there will be many cases in which a proportion has been paid back by the borrower, but there will be all

sorts of variants. The principle is simply this: the government is standing back of fifteen per cent of the total loans by any institution as a whole, and that institution cannot receive from the government under any circumstances more than a sum equivalent to fifteen per cent of the amount of its loans. speechtext: In order to be brief, I will refer only to section 6, clause (e), which states that no service or insurance charges shall be made as long as the borrower is not in default. Is the matter of the penalty to be imposed upon the debtor to be left entirely in the hands of the manager of the lending institution?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext: No.

subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext: There is nothing, in my opinion, which defines the point. subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS

[Mr. Dunning.l
home. He contracts for the making of those alterations and the contractor fails to make good. The mechanics file liens, and a new situation develops. What is the position so far as this measure is concerned, and what is the position of the government in regard to that new situation?

subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS

subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext:
Section 6(c) of the bill reads, in part:
Home improvement loans shall be for a term not exceeding three years if the amount of the loan is one thousand dollars or less,
I fancy that a good many small-salaried home owners will apply for some assistance. In case any such man should find himself without an income, say two years after he took out the loan, would there be any attempt on the part of financial institutions to refinance the balance over another three years? Would that be permitted, or not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext: That can be covered in the regulations.

subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext:
Section 6, clause (d), reads:
The maximum charge which may be made by an approved lending institution for a home improvement loan shall not exceed a rate of discount of three and one-quarter per centum for a one year loan repayable in equal monthly instalments and proportionate rates for other periods;
Two nights ago we found on our desks an attractive little pamphlet, and1 I became interested in what it contains. I find in it statements with regard to the organization of certain committees. One of these is the financial committee. The statement reads:
The financial committee raises whatever necessary money may be required for advertising and other local expenses. One of the functions of that committee is to investigate the number of possible homes in the community where improvement might well be carried out. In order that the various supply houses, contracting firms, building organizations may get a clear idea of rvhat the market for improvement is in that locality, and see at a glance its value to them, the financial committee should be ready to advise all of these supply houses as to how to approach the householder, estimate the work to be done and arrange-if necessary- for the householder to be accompanied to the bank when the loan is arranged. In some parts of the United States it was found that the contractors and supply houses (such, for

Home Improvement Loans
instance, as those manufacturing paints, heating and plumbing supplies, roofing materials, etc.) were the great gatherers-in of the people and their loans. The financial committee, ho%vever, might be reminded that this movement is for the improvement of people's houses and not a movement to induce people to borrow money from the bank. The bank borrowings are simply a convenient form of accomplishing the main objective, which is to get men employed through improvement of the home.
There seems to me to be some conflict there. Next we come to the women's committee, and we find:
They exercise the greatest amount of influence in persuading the family to spend the family dollar for improvement of the home. The national women's organizations are interested in the project and whatever branches of these national organizations are located in the municipality might well be used. It is not necessary to emphasize the importance, therefore, of choosing a chairman who is sympathetic with this plan, as well as representative of social and welfare work.
Under the heading "Trouble Committee" we find the following:
As a general thing, the chairman should be one of the most solid business men in the community, who enjoys the confidence of the banks, who is sympathetic with this idea, and who has broad human sympathies.
I have been wondering whether there is very much cooperation there. As I understood this bill the other day, before you can get a loan you must satisfy the lending institution. The lending institution must have perfect confidence in you; you must be of good character and you must have a job with an assured salary and a home. The man without a salary or without a home is not in on this deal at all, but only the man whose salary is assured, who has a home and has sufiicient credit to go ahead on his own. But 1 would refer to a particular type of man who might come under this legislation, the man who receives a salary just sufficient to get by on and to pay his taxes or his rent as the case may be, and whose home is also mortgaged. In a bank the other day I was told that possibly seventy-five per cent of the people under this plan have mortgaged homes. Under this plan no security is needed, but there is no guarantee whatever that as soon as the improvements are made and the loan is repaid the mortgage company, if the man defaults, will not take the house after it has all been fixed up and the payments have been made to the financial institution. There is no cooperation whatever as far as the lending institutions are concerned.
Borrowers may obtain money at a discount of 3i per cent. I think it might be better to put it the way people are accustomed to see it stated-an interest rate of 6.32 per cent.
That does not show any cooperation, because it is very little below the legal rate at which the banks may lend money. I suggest that instead of the 3i per cent the discount be reduced to 2 per cent; the banks would thus be given an opportunity to cooperate in a practical manner. If this is not satisfactory, then I suggest that the country's credit might be used, and we might make use of the Bank of Canada in this regard. This would be far better business than following the sound money policy which is adhered to in this plan.

subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext:
There are three points which I wish to draw to the attention of the minister. The definition of home improvement loan is given in paragraph (b) of section 2:
(b) "home improvement loan" means a loan or a purchase of obligations representing loans and advances of money made for the purpose of financing repairs, alterations and additions to rural and urban homes.
It may be rather late to suggest any change here, but I would ask that the minister consider the possibility of amending this definition so as to include the building of small homes. I have in mind some people in Rosthern who might build small homes that would cost say $1,500, which would provide as much labour by an expenditure of the same amount in improving an old home. But they cannot come under the scheme if they want to put up new houses. I suggest that some consideration be given such people.
There is another point namely with respect to default. When there is default and the bank calls upon the government to make good, what becomes of the debt? There is no provision in the bill to enable the government to collect later on if the debtor should become able to pay. I submit that the bill should contain some provision in that respect, because there might be a doubt.

subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext:
It would be recovered by
process of law.

subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext: There might be some doubt about it, and I do not see that there is any harm in making provision for it in the regulations.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext: What about paragraph (b) of section 8?

subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext:
I submit it does not cover the point at all in the event of default and the payment of the guarantee by the government. In my opinion the government's position is not secured by paragraph (b) of section 8, and I submit that it should be madJe clear.
The third point to which I wish to call attention is this. I understand, from para-
Home Improvement Loans

graph (e) of section 6, that no service or insurance charges shall be made by a lending institution at any time, and as long as the borrower is not in default no additional charges of any kind shall be made. That section is not worded very clearly. I assume the intention is that no service or insurance charges are to be made at any time, whether the borrower is in default or not, but that after the borrower is in default some charges other than for service or insurance may be made. What I think the government must have had in mind1 is that an interest charge be made. I understand from the minister that there is a clause in the regulations providing that interest may be charged not exceeding seven per cent. The difficulty is that there is no provision in section 8 for fixing that interest charge.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext: In section 8 provision is made with respect to the form of note, and what shall be in it.

subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext: Well, there is nothing in section 8 that says it very definitely. If it is the intention to restrict the lending institutions merely to charging interest, to keep them from piling up other charges, there should be something put in to the effect that when the borrower is in default no additional charges of any kind shall be made except interest on the amount overdue at a rate not exceeding that fixed: by regulation under section 8. That would make it certain that they could not charge anything but interest, and would give the minister power to fix the rate. Those are the three suggestions I offer.

subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext: There is one observation I was about to make before the last member spoke. This guarantee is given by the government but it is not a guarantee against default. The guarantee has really no exact relationship to default.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext: To ultimate loss only.

subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext: The guarantee is against ultimate loss. Before the ultimate loss of the bank in respect of any single loan can be determined the bank must exercise all its legal rights in respect to the collection of that loan. I suggest that the bank would find it necessary to bring suit, to obtain judgment, and to execute the judgment upon whatever property the borrower may own. Therefore no liability arises on the part of the government until the bank has made a loan, there has been default by the borrower, and the bank has exercised all its legal rights for the collection of the loan, and after exercising all its rights of recovery it has been ascertained that there is a definite specific loss.

subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext: Is not the hon. member ignoring the provisions of section 8 (b), which states that the minister may, with the approval of the governor in council, make regulations governing the method of determining the amount of loss? The hon. gentleman assumes that there is to be an action and judgment, that the loss has to be determined in a certain way. But I should think from the wording of this provision that the minister with the approval of the governor in council may provide that a loss may be determined by a method shorter than or different from that outlined by the hon. member.

subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext:
Suppose a borrower
goes to a lending institution, and his proposal to borrow a sum of money is accepted, will he get the money and be able to take it awTay with him, or will the money be paid by the institution only when he produces receipts showing it was expended as it was supposed to be? Suppose the property is an apartment house containing twenty apartments. If the owner could borrow' SI .000 on each and go out with the money in his hand, what guarantee has the lending institution that the money will be spent as it was the intention it should be?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext: That is the business of the lending institution in determining the credit-worthiness of the person who borrows the money. I cannot say anything other than that.

subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext: But the government undertakes to make good some of that money. That point has been worrying me. I assume the lending institution would protect itself, but at the same time in case of loss the government would be out a certain amount of money. It seems to me the government should have some way of knowing that the money actually goes into the enterprise.

subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext: The answer is that the lending institution has an eighty-five per cent interest as against a possible fifteen per cent on the part of the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext:
We have penalties, but that may not be considered much protection. The chief protection, after all, is the fact mentioned by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett), that the lending institution, assuming there is a one hundred per cent loss, will lose eighty-five per cent. And in the event of any crookedness, you could not assume that after something improper had been done the man who did it would repay eighty-five per cent. Any policing in the manner suggested by the hon. member for St.

Home Improvement Loans
Boniface (Mr. Howden) would, I am sure, cost more than would be practicable. This scheme involves hundreds of thousands of small loans. As I said the other day, the average loan so far is $380. To contemplate the setting up of inspection machinery to ensure that an average loan of $380 is spent precisely for the objects for which it was granted-it is unthinkable.

subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext: They might have to appoint inspectors under the civil service commission.

subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext:
That is not the whole
point. There is still the question not only of the money not being repaid but of its not going into the enterprise for which it was borrowed.

subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext: There is that possibility.

subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext: It occurs to me that since the bank is guaranteed up to fifteen per cent it will make every effort to collect the eighty-five per cent. But has the government any guarantee that it will make the same effort to collect the remaining fifteen per cent? I ask that in view of the reputation which has been given to the banks in this house in the last three or four weeks; it causes me to doubt whether they would exercise the same care in collecting money for the government as they would for themselves.

subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext:
It seems to me the first
question to decide is whether or not the power to prepare regulations is extensive enough to enable the regulations to be prepared, and, second, what kind of regulations shall be prepared.

subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext:
And what is their effect.
They have no legal effect under this bill.

subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext:
If the first point is
dealt with adequately, the second also will be dealt with adequately. The first question that suggests itself to me is: What are the provisions of the agreement between the lending institution and the guarantor, the government, as to what is to be the result of default; (a) as to granting further time- that has been covered by what has been done here to-day; (b) as to the effect of default in payment of one instalment upon others. Shall the others come due, for instance? And it seems to me the third question to be decided, after you have settled those, is, shall the position of the guarantor, the government, be that of the bank as soon as default has been made, and payment of eightydive per cent of the aggregate loan provided; shall the bank make an assignment to the government of its position-that is,
shall there be subrogation, and is there any provision for it? I cannot conceive of anything worse than that the government should be mixed up in any sense in the matter of endeavouring to collect fifteen per cent of $380 in various parts of this country. I say that very frankly; I think it would be an absurd position. Then that question of the agreement between the bank and the guarantor is the all-important question on that side of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext: Agreed.

subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext:
I say this with deference, but I think the Department of Justice can take section 8 and make it clearer than it is now. The point made by the hon. member for Rosthern, it seems to me, should be dealt with clearly by making it apparent in the statute itself that while the loan is not in default no charge is to be made for anything except such charges as are provided by that statute.
Or the second point, in view of the recent decisions of the privy council I do not see how we can possibly go so far as to say that the bank, in its relations with its debtors, cannot do as it pleases when they are in default. Mark you, we do not make the loan; the bank makes the loan, and the rights as between the bank and the man who borrows from the bank have not been changed by anything we are doing. All we do is to say that when there is a loss of fifteen per cent in the aggregate of the loans thus made, we will pay fifteen per cent. That is the whole story. We have not substituted our discretion for that of the bank manager. He still has to be accountable to his head office for his discretion, as he always has been. He still has to determine whether or not it is a good risk to take, morally, and whether the character behind it is worth while. The only thing he does not do is to require security. It may be that the property is mortgaged; in many cases that will be so. The very reason this measure is being brought in is to enable some of those cases to be dealt with.
We must bear in mind, I say to the hon. member for St. Boniface, that the government cannot possibly police these loans. It would be idle to expect the government to have some one running around to see that fifteen per cent of a loan of $300, which amounts to $45, is being properly spent; for our responsibility in connection with that fifteen per cent would involve the spending of more than that amount in connection with inspection. If we did it on the basis of patronage I imagine it would be very desirable in some ways. I see my hon. friend from York North
Home Improvement Loans

smiling. He lives near a large urban riding, and he would have a great many inspectors to appoint, but the civil service commission will look after that.
Leaving that aside for the moment, however, I think we should look upon this as a remedial measure which must be construed in the widest possible way. All that happens is that somebody goes into a bank and applies for a loan to be paid back within a specified time in monthly instalments. The bank has to do what all banks have done heretofore; it has to determine whether or not it will take the risk, and the only thing that makes this transaction at all out of the ordinary is that we say that if the banker makes a bad guess, and has not taken security-or as we say he shall not-at some time we are going to pay fifteen per cent. I think there should be a cut-off date specified, as was suggested by the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling), but in any case we say that we will pay fifteen per cent.

subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext: Of the aggregate.

subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext: Of course. That is the story.

subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext: That is much different.

subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext: Of course, because there might be a one hundred per cent loss in one place which would be made up by a one hundred per cent recovery in another place. That, I take it, is why the minister has made it the aggregate.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext: The administrative cost of the other method would put it completely out of court.

subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext:
Quite so. That is the position, and I think section 8 can be improved to the extent of making it clearer than it now is that the granting of power to the government to enact legislation by order in council is sufficiently ample to satisfy every reasonable requirement in an agreement between the lending institutions and the government.
While I am on my feet I direct attention to the fact that the government have seen fit to depart from that great principle upon which the whole foundation of responsible government is built, by making provision for taking money out of the consolidated revenue without any appropriation. That is a catastrophe. If you have any doubt on that subject, Mr. Chairman, I recommend that you read the speeches of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie) King) at any time during the period from 1930 to 1935, together with a few caustic comments by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill).

subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext: There is one question I should like to ask the minister in regard to these guarantees. Let us suppose that a man repays fifty per cent of the loan and then defaults and pays nothing further. This loss is included in the amount which the government ultimately guarantees and pays. Does that mean that the original owner of the property who has made the improvements and who owns them pays nothing further for them, or does the lending institution step in and obtain possession of the property while the government still has to make up the loss? That is rather a tangled sort of question; it is over-simplification on my part, .but cases of that kind will arise, and: I should like to know what will be the position.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext:
Let me see if I can
follow my hon. friend's supposition. A borrower repays fifty per cent, and he does not pay anything more. Then the question is to determine whether or not that is an ultimate loss. The regulations must provide that the bank shall take all reasonable measures of collection having regard to the amount to be collected. The bank would not be allowed to engage the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, for instance, to prosecute in the case of a $50 debt, or my hon. friend the Minister of National Revenue, or any other lawyer whose employment would involve expense greater than would be reasonable in connection with thie collection of such a small amount.

subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext:
Why deprive them of
good lawyers?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext: I am advised that one of the first things good lawyers learn is how to charge.

subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext: Are high charges made only by good lawyers?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext: That is not a question to address to me, and I prefer to be excused from answering it. But if I can make it clear to my hon. friend from Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) this is the whole point: Is the remaining $50 lost?

subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext: Fifty per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext:
Yes; that is $50 on a loan of $100. The regulations must provide a manner of determining definitely that it is lost. The government does not propose to pay its guarantee without being sure that every reasonable method has been adopted to avoid loss and to collect everything that can be collected. But on the other hand that does not

mean that we would encourage the expenditure of a greater amount than the sum to be collected in an attempt to recover that sum.

subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext: The member for the constituency will look after that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS

subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext: But your literature says he will be the first man in it.

subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext:
There is nothing in this measure that provides for any expenditure on or any charge by the lawyer. That evidently did not enter into the contemplation of those who drew up this bill. Where the loss arises is in respect of a loan, and a proportion of the loan being lost. At the moment I wish to state simply that I cannot accept the construction placed upon section 8(b) by the Minister of National Revenue. I think when these sections are reconsidered by the Department of Justice the point I made should be taken into consideration, because loss is not necessarily incurred upon default. As the minister now admits, the loss is the net loss after reasonable remedies have been taken to recover the loan in whole or in part. Paragraph (b) does not clearly refer to the measures to be taken and the procedure to be followed. These are not apt words, I suggest, to determine what remedies are to be taken. I think the word "procedure" is not sufficient to govern, and, second, regulations made by order in council have no more force in law than regulations made by the minister or by any individual. No provision is made which gives these regulations the force of law, and that omission should certainly be considered.
I disagree with my right hon. leader in this respect, that I consider the making of these regulations is not legislation by the government, because in this measure the government have not taken any authority to give force of law to the regulations they make. Such regulations, if made undter this section, would, I suggest, be so much waste paper.

speechtext:
Shall section 6 as

speechtext: No.

speechtext: I thought it was to stand.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext:
It would be well to let sections 6 and 8 stand. Section 6 is amended to this point. We shall permit sections 6 and 8 to stand, in order that I may again take up the suggestions with the Department of Justice. In deference to the officers of the
department may I say to the committee that in drafting the bill they have had the advantage of watching the actual problems arise after two months' administration of the plan, and have had the further advantage of seeing the experience in the United States in the administration of a similar program. Of course, as always, I am in the hands of my official legal advisers with respect to the ultimate drafting of the measure. I thought it well to invite the committee, and particularly the legal members of it, to make suggestions, and such suggestions I shall be glad' to refer to the proper department. The measure will be returned at a later date with such further amendments or reasons for not amending it as may commend themselves to the law officers.
If that arrangement is satisfactory, and if hon. members are content with the discussion thus far on section 6, we shall allow it to stand, with the amendments made. When we reach section 8, I shall be pleased to allow it to stand1 also, in order that the points raised by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George in connection with paragraph (b) may be considered.

subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext: Of course the law officers have hadi nothing to do with the question of default. We are now talking about remedies. They have not yet had anything to do with them, I hope.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext: It is a little early for that.

subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext: Does the minister consider there is any conflict between paragraphs (c) and (d)? In paragraph (c) the expression is "and shall be repayable in convenient periodic instalments," and in paragraph (d) it is "repayable in equal monthly instalments." I raise the point because committees in Saskatchewan have been endeavouring to interest farmers in this important plan, and on every occasion we are met with the statement that farmers are not in receipt of a monthy income, and! that their income is periodic. Therefore they would like to have a plan which would permit payment every two, three, four or five months. On reading paragraph (c), it occurred to me that that was the intention, but in paragraph (d) there is a reference to repayment "in equal monthly instalments."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext:
I think the hon. member has misread the paragraph. Paragraph (d) sets up a maximum charge. In order to set up such maximum charge, the time of repayment must be specified. The hon. member will note the paragraph continues with the

Home Improvement Loans

words "and proportionate rates for other periods." The three and a quarter per cent discount with respect to a one year loan is the measuring stick by which the discount rate to be charged for all other periods must be measured,. That is the reason for paragraph (d) following (c). With regard to loans made under repayment conditions varying from the monthly period, may I tell the hon. member that in rural districts many loans are now being made in which the periods of repayment are being adjusted to the expected intomes of the farmers. But the measuring stick is to the discount rate is paragraph (d), and such discount rate must not exceed a rate of three and a quarter per cent when payments are monthly.
Mr. O'NEILL:	Has it been found impossible or impracticable to determine the loss in each individual case or to judge each individual case by itself, in place of judging all cases in the aggregate ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext:
Each individual case will be dealt with by itself, but the application of the guarantee will be based upon the total sum lost, spread over all the loans. In one case the loss of the bank may be 100 per cent; in another case it may be only ten per cent, while in another there may be no loss at all. Each case must be proved. But in measuring the extent to which we will repay the lending institution, fifteen per cent of the total they loan is the limit to which the repayment may go.
Mr. O'NEILL: That is clear. The way it appears to me, however, is that by this manner of reckoning the government will have to pay more money than they would if they paid fifteen per cent on the loss which takes place in each case. If a man paid back 100 per cent, this would be all right, but if he paid back only fifty per cent they would be paying only on a fifty per cent loss. If he did not pay anything, the government would pay the fifteen per cent. When we reckon the whole thing in the aggregate, it seems to me that in most cases the government will have to pay. After everything is said and done, they will be paying nearly all the loss. I am not a banker, but that is the way it appears to me.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext:
In that connection I can only advance the experience of the United States. They have a plan which involves a twenty per cent government guarantee, carrying a five per cent discount rate, or a rate almost double that in Canada, and after three years of operation their aggregate losses are
\Mr. Dunning.]
less than two per cent. This is a new venture, so far as we are concerned, but it would appear from the experience in the United States that the hon. member's fears are apparently unfounded.

But the position there is vastly different.

Section 8 stands.

subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS

speechtext:
This brings up the point
I mentioned. Why cannot this bill be made to apply to a man who wants to borrow money with which to build a new home? In the constituency which I have the honour to represent there are people who own lots who have said to me that the only interest they have in this bill is the possibility of being able to borrow money to put up a small new home. If the idea is to promote employment, I cannot see why the bill should not be made to apply to the man who wants to borrow to put up a new home.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext: It would require a different statute altogether to provide for housing. In my judgment it would be quite impracticable to combine housing with home improvement. The situation in each case is quite different.

subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext:
Has the government any
intention of amending at this session of parliament the present housing act?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext:
I am afraid my hon.
friend will have to wait for an answer to that question.

subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext: I do not want to disagree too much with the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext:
The hon. member is at
perfect liberty to do that; that is his privilege.

subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext:
The basis of this bill is
the personal liability of the individual borrowing the money. If a man is good for $2,000

Home Improvement Loans
to improve a house, why should not a man who owns a lot be good for a similar amount to build a new house? I cannot see how this would complicate matters, although I may be overlooking something. The government says to the banks that it will guarantee up to fifteen per cent of the loans made, providing the money is used to improve existing houses. How would it complicate things to say that the government will also guarantee loans made if the money is used to build a new house? What, in essence, is the difference between a man borrowing $2,000 to put up a little house on a lot which he owns, and a man borrowing $2,000 to improve his house? The same employment will be created. A man may have a home worth only $500 and may want to borrow money to improve it to make it worth $2,000. The question of security does not enter into the matter as the loans are to be based entirely upon the personal obligation of the borrower. All that is needed to make this bill apply to loans for new buildings is two small alterations in sections 2 and 10. I do not believe that during the next three years there will be expended under this act anything like the $50,000,000 expected, but if the legislation were made to apply to new buildings I am sure there would be twice as much expended as will be the case under the act as it stands. The idea is to provide employment and I think consideration should be given to this matter. Several people in Rosthern constituency have said to me that if they could borrow $2,000 they would erect new homes on lots which they already own. This bill as it is now will be of no use to them at all. If this bill is worth while, it should be worth while giving consideration to the extension in its scope in the way I have mentioned.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS

I can only repeat what I said before, that the principle is an entirely different one. It would involve the consideration of many factors other than those which apply in the case of home improvement. with respect to property and civil rights and all that sort of thing. For instance, this is something that occurs to me as a layman and I put it to my hon. friend who is a lawyer. on it. I know of no difficulty in the law of the provinces standing in the way, although I may be wrong. If a difficulty can be pointed out, I am ready to defer to it.

subtopic: REVISION OF ACCOUNTING SET-UP

speechtext:
Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Transport) moved the second reading of Bill No. 12, to provide for revision of the accounting set-up of the Canadian National railway system.
He said: A complete explanation of the purpose of the bill was given, I think, in committee on the resolution. At that time I stated that one purpose was to consolidate the component parts of the Canadian National system into one balance sheet. I think the importance of that action cannot be discounted. At the time of the Duff report the component parts of the system included some 130 separate corporations. Since then the number has been reduced to about 100 separate corporations, and the work of further reducing these numbers will be made considerably easier if all parts can be consolidated in one corporation. This the bill will effect.

subtopic: REVISION OF ACCOUNTING SET-UP
speechtext:
Surely that is not what
this bill is. The minister is not serious in saying that this bill consolidates the constituents in one corporation.

subtopic: REVISION OF ACCOUNTING SET-UP
speechtext:
We shall say that it brings
them into one holding company with one balance sheet.

subtopic: REVISION OF ACCOUNTING SET-UP
speechtext:
But the balance sheet
issued by the Canadian National Railways is a single balance sheet.

subtopic: REVISION OF ACCOUNTING SET-UP
speechtext:
It is; nevertheless there are
at the present time three separate corporations. As I explained, the Canadian National Railways as a corporate structure includes the old Grand Trunk railway and some sixty of its subsidiary companies, and quite a separate corporation is the Canadian Northern Railway Company with some forty subsidiaries. It is a separate corporation in every way, the stock of which is owned by the Minister of Finance, just as the stock of the Canadian National Railways is owned by the Minister of Finance. There is no connection between the two corporations except that they have a common board of directors. As I pointed out before, owing to the fact that the government does its financing, and its refunding as well, for both corporations, through the Canadian National Railways, the debt of the Canadian Northern is being gradually transferred to the Canadian National Railway Company, an entirely distinct and separate corporation. As I say, this bill will bring these roads under
one control and the board of directors of the Canadian National Railways will be ipso facto the board of directors of what is now the Canadian Northern railway. The Canadian Northern Railway Company will disappear as a separate entity.
With respect to the writing down of the accounts of the railway, I may say that the bill, which has been distributed, is susceptible of analysis as to just what is contemplated in that regard. As to the discussion of the details of the bill, I believe the standing committee is the proper forum for the purpose. Expert accountants will be in attendance and it will be possible for the committee to go minutely into the various items that are set out. I took little exception to the remarks of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) when the resolution was being considered in committee. He then pointed out that a record should be kept of the sums invested by the dominion in its railways. In my opinion the method of doing this is one which must engage the attention of the committee. It is perfectly clear that, once we set up a balance sheet which cannot be questioned as to what is intended, this balance sheet should not be' beclouded by reference to items which are now a part of the national debt and which will be so treated. I believe a schedule can be set up that will preserve the historical record, and this schedule can be made part of the annual report of the Canadian National Railways. That perhaps will satisfy the purpose as to a record.
I do not believe anyone will question the fact that the duplication as between the railway accounts and the public accounts should be eliminated. There may be those who take a different view as to the manner in which this duplication should be eliminated, but in my opinion there are only two ways in which this can be done; one is to take the duplicated items out of the railway account and the other is to take them out of the consolidated debt of Canada account. By taking a billion and a half out of the consolidated debt we could render the task of the Minister of Finance very much easier for this particular year.

The interest has to be

subtopic: REVISION OF ACCOUNTING SET-UP
speechtext:
It would give him a substantial credit in his next annual budget. I believe that a great deal of misunderstanding arises through duplication. The intelligent taxpayer of Canada is naturally concerned as to what his taxes are used for.
C.N.R.-Accounting-Mr. Howe

He is told that a certain proportion of the taxes goes to the servicing of the national [DOT]debt. He is then informed that the losses of the Canadian National Railways in cash are [DOT]so much; that is, that the taxes of the current year are charged a certain amount to make up the sum which must be turned over to the Canadian National Railways to keep it going. In addition to that, he learns that a mysterious sum shown in the statement of the railways is also a liability, and I believe most of the confusion with respect to the true position arises in connection with this additional sum shown as a loss which the railway does not pay. When the annual statement is brought down, there are newspapers that carry an alarming story about the situation disclosed by the account of $40,000,000 or $50,000,000 charged up to the system, and most people have the idea that there is some intermediate amount somewhere between the amount they are taxed to service the national debt and the amount they are taxed to hand over to the railway for its losses. If this bill passes as drawn there will be no longer a question about that intermediate amount; the taxpayer will know that when he services the national debt and provides funds to be turned over to the railway for the indebtedness which must be paid by them, the whole story has been told as far as the position of the dominion and its taxpayers is concerned.
Some extraordinary charges are made with regard to this situation. A few weeks ago there appeared in Ottawa a man, a student of railway affairs, who used some extraordinary language about this proposed adjustment of the balance sheet. He spoke of "perfidy, to the public welfare," of "votes of the unthinking masses," of "pure deception," a "dissembling of the real facts," and "political debauchery run riot." I cannot think that there is anything in what we are doing to warrant any of these charges. The operation is a perfectly simple one. We are removing this duplication between the public accounts and the accounts of the Canadian National Railways, the latter being the property of the taxpayers of Canada. I do not think I need dwell on this any longer.
As I have said, the exact method of carrying out the intention of the bill will come under the complete review of the committee, who will report back to the house. The record of exactly what has been spent by the public in connection with the railways may tell a story, but it is by no means a cofnplete story of what the public has spent on transportation. I have had a review made of the public accounts showing appropria-
LMr. Howe.]
tions for transportation, and in this connection I wish to make this statement. In the situation of transportation to-day it is hardly fair to single out the railways for treatment different from that given any other form of transportation. Whereas twenty years ago the railways were the dominant factor in transportation-they then carried so large a percentage of the whole that the amount transported by other means was not very important-to-day the railways are only one factor in transportation and no longer the dominant factor.
In looking over the public accounts I find that from time to time sums up to $1,506,000,000 have been advanced to the component parts of the Canadian National railways and to that railway itself. That sum is without interest; the interest, I suppose, would amount to about another $600,000,000. I also find that the sum of $104,000,000 has been paid in cash to the Canadian Pacific railway and written off. The interest on that, as it goes back a great many years, would have been perhaps another $300,000,000.

speechtext:
No; they are in shipping. So as far as the record of the sums invested in the Canadian National Railways is concerned, I do not believe that is so important in the general scheme of things except for one reason, namely that this railway is competing with a privately owned railway which stands on its own feet. We must not forget that prior to the war we had three privately owned railways in Canada; to-day we have only one. The reason we have a problem with our own railway is largely that the other two privately owned railways were not able to meet the situation brought on by the war. 1 think in fairness to its private competitor that record should be kept, and I believe a way will be found by the committee to set up a record in a manner that will meet the suggestions which have been made along that line.
Something was said about the position of the South African railways. Their position is extraordinarily favourable for a government owned utility. But I wonder whether the people of Canada would be satisfied to have our railway operated along similar lines. First, we must remember that the South African railway has a complete monopoly, while our railway operation is highly competitive. In 1935 the South African railway was able to obtain a surplus of $27,000,000 after interest charges were paid and a charge of $10,000,000 made for depreciation, while in the same year the Canadian National Railways had a cash deficit of .$47,000,000 after payment of interest due to the public but not to the government. We find also that the revenue per mile of the South African railway was $11,061, whereas the revenue per mile of the Canadian National is only $7,322; in other words the revenue per mile of the South African railway is 50 per cent greater than on the Canadian National Railways. If we could somehow obtain a 50 per cent increase in revenue per mile we could not only meet our debt to the public but have a small surplus in addition. Expressing it in another way, we contribute the amount to the public in the way of low freight rates, the lowest in the world, rather than have the surplus which the South African railway enjoys. I might also mention that the employees of the South African railways are about 30 per cent native, or non-European.

subtopic: REVISION OF ACCOUNTING SET-UP
speechtext: More than that.

subtopic: REVISION OF ACCOUNTING SET-UP
speechtext:
But to me this is the interesting thing about South Africa: I wish it
were something that the public would take note of seriously. One provision of their railway act is that the mileage of 11,292 miles operated by the government is protected against wasteful and uneconomic competition in areas adequately served by the railway. Such areas are defined by proclamation under their Motor Carrier Transportation Act. Even taxis cannot operate a regular service between particular places without permission. I wonder whether our people would be satisfied with that. To-day Canadians have the option of travel by rail or motor. If the house thinks they do not, appreciate both, hon. members might examine some of the cases heard before the railway board where the railways wished to abandon a branch line, where all the traffic was going to the trucks. In South Africa, if a community has a railway, or if a railway serves any section, service by any other means is absolutely prohibited.
Yet it is interesting to note that the writing off of capital is a live subject there, as it is here. In the report of 1935 it is stated that:
The board of management have asked the government to reduce the capitalization by some $110,000,000 covering costs prior to union.
We come to the Australian railways, and find there a much more serious situation than in South Africa, quite as serious, I think, as we have in Canada.

subtopic: REVISION OF ACCOUNTING SET-UP
speechtext: Except that they are state systems, not one system.

Mr. Speaker, in view of what the minister has said as to the intention to leave to the special committee a large measure of discretion in dealing with the legislation, I shall confine myself to dealing with two questions.
The first is the distinct differences between the bill and the address delivered by the minister when he moved the resolution. In my judgment the bill does violence to sound principles of finance, and I cannot think the

minister seriously expects the committee to adopt the bill as it stands. I have just sent for the report of the Canadian National Railways for the year ended December 31, 1935. That is what I say. Therefore this item, namely the long term debt item, stands at $1,154,779,000.78.
The next item in the liability column is: Loans from the Dominion of Canada: temporary loans obtained for redemption of funded debt, pending refunding interest paid, $74,726,975. This is an item which varies from time to time as the government carries on refunding operations for the railway when its obligations mature and a lower rate of interest is obtained, and as far as this item is concerned it cannot be modified or changed. It stands.
The next item is the important one: Other loans from Dominion of Canada, $679,873,935.08. Interest on above accrued but unpaid, $495,030,137.29, or a total of $1,174,904,072.37. I deny the right of this parliament, in honest dealing with the public, to change this amount by a single cent. It represents money paid by the Canadian people into the capital of this enterprise; it represents loans from the Dominion of Canada. The dominion government went into the open market and borrowed money, and then lent it to the Canadian National, that is, the constituent companies which now comprise the Canadian National. The money was not given by way of subsidy. Let us not have any misunderstanding about that. It was not given by way of subsidy or subvention; it was not given by way of special advances for capital stock, as in the case of the old Canadian Northern. It represents loans made to the railways of Canada. My submission is that it stands in a position where it should not be changed even by one cent. Why? Because it represents loans made to the enterprises as going concerns. Just as the minister has said, these roads represent a combination of two privately owned systems and, he might have said, one of the difficulties the people of Canada have in dealing with the railways is that those roads were not constructed by a common proprietor, but were constructed by competing proprietors. Many of them were not built in such a way as to make it possible for them to yield a revenue, when combined with the other competing system. In other words, the Canadian Pacific railway was laid out, according to the plan of its proprietors, where they thought traffic was available. In the case of the other railways, one was a contractors' road, built for subsidies, and the other was built afterwards- and never should have been built-for the
purpose of endeavouring to make a connection with the Grand Trunk system, between the east and the west.
These are important points to keep in mind when we are considering our position with respect to our railways. But, to get back to the financial statement: Why should we change a single cent or word of it? This is a certified report, submitted by trustees and certified by auditors. First, " loans from Dominion of Canada"; should that be written off?

speechtext: I am coming to that presently. At the moment I am considering the accounts. These represent moneys the Canadian people borrowed on their credit, and lent to the railways. There is no duplication in that. If I may use the term with respect, I would say that it is absurd to use the word "duplication" in referring to two separate entities which are keeping their separate accounts, the one borowing from the other. The accounts of the Dominion of Canada show what we owe the world. Our accounts show that we owe the world hundreds of millions of dollars. The accounts of the Canadian National Railways show that they owe us hundreds of millions of dollars which they borrowed from us when we, the Canadian people, borrowed money from the world. There is no duplication in that. Every person knows that is the way in which accounts are kept in every enterprise in the world. One enterprise shows where it got the money and, in turn, the other enterprise shows where it got the money. In its public accounts the Dominion of Canada shows that it borrowed money from people throughout the world who lend it. The Canadian National Railways borrowed from us, the people of Canada. I do not think it would
be fair to the dominion to compare the conditions in South Africa with those in Canada. It is unfair to Canada because in South Africa native labour is a very important item in their operations and they are able, therefore, to operate their system at a very much lower cost relatively than we are. In addition to that, they have, as the minister pointed out, a complete monopoly of traffic, whereas under the railway department we have the railways, the airways, the harbours, the highways and certain steamships, all of which constitutes a condition that is not comparable with that which prevails in South Africa. One phase of the operation of the South African railways that does appeal to me, however, is the efficiency of the operation. When I said the other day that out of their gross earnings, that is, before charging depreciation, only 58 per cent, and that after charging depreciation, only a little over 65-42 per cent of their earnings was required to maintain the system, leaving a substantial balance for other purposes, I indicated a condition which I think approximates perfection as nearly as possible in operations in these days. But the real, the essential fact is the difference with respect to labour costs. Of total earnings of the South African railways last year, only 38-13 was spent for labour. And that is the whole story; when you have stated that you have stated practically the whole of it. Comparing that with conditions in Canada, you find on page 4 of the report of last year that the operating ratio for 1935 was 91-77 per cent as compared with 92-14 per cent in 1934. Then follow the particulars of the expenditures that were made. As is known, of course, the labour cost involved was substantially twice what it was in South Africa; the figures are given in the report, but I will not take the time to deal with them.
There is only one other point I should like to bring to the minister's attention, and it is this. He cannot possibly say that the consolidated balance sheet of the railways- and I direct his attention to pages 16 and 17 of the report-is not a fairly complete report of the position of the system. If that is true- and I think it must be taken to be-why should we disallow any of the items contained in that balance sheet other than the ones I have mentioned? It cannot be claimed that there is duplication, because that balance sheet does not in any sense duplicate any report in connection with the national debt.

C.N.R.-Accounting-Mr. Bennett
It cannot be said to be misleading so far as our credit is concerned, for it deals in extreme detail with the whole situation, setting out in succeeding pages the details of every issue that was made by the railway company and also borrowings from the Dominion of Canada. Loans from the Dominion of Canada will be found on page 29 of last year's report. These loans from the dominion make up a total of over $669,000,000 in addition to the sums required for financing last year. Why should we in any sense lessen these amounts in any balance sheet we prepare?
I am perfectly willing to be convinced-* I have no feeling about the matter-but I believe that in fairness and in justice to the Canadian people we should make clear to them what the position is. Let me put to the minister one difficulty that has arisen by reason of the very statements made by him and others in this chamber. It has been suggested that the cash deficit last year was $48,000,000. That is not the fact. The Canadian taxpayer had to find $48,000,000 on income deficit, that is, on the income not being able to meet, not the interest on the money which the Canadian people had put into the enterprise but the interest on the securities which the Canadian National had issued, not those that represented money borrowed from the Canadian people on their general credit as part of the national debt. That is made abundantly clear by the report itself. Why, then, should we say that the deficit was $48,000,000? We know it was twice that. Why? Because the taxpayer had to pay the interest on the money which the dominion borrowed and lent to the Canadian Northern, and that is not included in the $48,000,000.
Let me make the situation perfectly clear so that there will be no misunderstanding about it. On page 28 we find the funded debt, principal and interest:
Total debt held by public (including therein $11,792,798.65 par value held in special funds and accounts) as per balance sheet	$1,154,779,000 78
That is the total debt incurred by the companies which are now under the Canadian National system, all set out in detail. That debt of $1,154,000,000 odd was incurred by the railway companies; the interest on it is payable by the companies, and they had $48,000,000 less than what was required to pay interest on that amount held by the public. But turn to the other side of the question and look at the page to which I directed attention, page 29, showing loans from the Dominion of Canada. The loans from the
Dominion of Canada being part of the national debt, the Canadian people are now paying interest on that debt. It has nothing at all to do with the $48,000,000; the amount of interest we paid last year on it came to the enormous sum of $35,949,676.70, as shown on page 29. So that, instead of $48,000,000, it was $48,000,000 plus $35,000,000, or $83,000,000, and that is in the report itself.

It was paid by the Canadian people to the people who held bonds of the Dominion of Canada with respect to some of the money lent to the Canadian National Railways. That is the story. Now, should we do anything with that which would make it appear to be other than it is? I say to the minister in all sincerity that he will find in these documents nothing which could give rise to any confusion. The auditors have made it so plain that the wayfaring man, though a fool, may read. He who runs may read; there it is. I want to go one step further, however. There are certain figures which the minister has used in his bill as indicating his intention, shall I say, to wipe out or write off sums representing the real debt of this system to the people of Canada since we began to operate the system. Why should that balance sheet be changed, then, if that is what these figures are, namely, an indication of the losses sustained by the Canadian people in the operation of their property since they nationalized it? That is my position.
The hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Bothwell) asked a question to which I now direct attention. He wanted to know whether in these figures I have given there was included any portion of the moneys paid by the dominion for deficits. There were included in those figures deficits up to 1932, but neither in this report, which is the report of the railway company, nor in the public accounts, is shown the extent to which the debt of Canada was expanded to provide money to pay deficits since 1932. So that there stand to be added to these figures the deficits that were paid by borrowing money in 1932. 1933. 1934, 1935 and 1936. These are not included and must be shown in any complete system of accounting.

Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Finance): Mr. Speaker, I desire to detain the house for only a few moments. The object of the government in proposing the legislation which the Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe) now has before us is not, as I think everyone will agree, to deceive the Canadian people or to produce a set of accounts for the Canadian National which will not reflect, as accurately as the complexities of the Canadian National system will permit, the true condition. My right hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) has just pronounced what I might term a doctrine of accounting perfection. No one can take exception to the broad general principles of accounting which he lays down, but with all respect may I point out that so far as the Canadian National balance sheet is concerned, the principles of accounting perfection were departed from quite a number of years ago, and have been departed from still further in the intervening years. I think it was back in 1920 or thereabouts when the difficulties incident to calculating the interest upon the unpaid interest on the money which had been advanced by the Canadian people to the Canadian National or its various units were a source of concern to the Minister of Finance of that day.

Quite obviously, if the Canadian people are required to advance money to pay interest upon money which was advanced by them to the railway, then interest on that interest is also payable from time to time by the Canadian people when it is not paid by the railway company. What the accumulation of that amount would be in the intervening years I am not going even to try to guess, but in any case, as far as the railway accounts were concerned, as far back as that the amount of interest due upon interest, which had been unpaid by the railway company to the Canadian people was dropped from consideration in the railway balance sheet. Later, my right hon. friend himself, facing the problem in 1932, I think, adopted the principle that in future the cash deficit should be paid out of the treasury of Canada.

It was a recommendation of the commission, and as my right hon. friend indicated this evening, since 1932 no accumulation of the amounts paid by the Minister of Finance with respect to the cash deficits of the Canadian National Railways has been added to the balance sheet items from year to year.
The point I am making is simply this, that with respect to an undertaking of such tremendous complexity, with the history which has been so well outlined by the Minister of Transport and the leader of the opposition, at this date it is impossible to lay down the principle of accounting perfection, apply it throughout all the years of the undertaking and expect to reach any intelligible result. The principle upon which the Minister of Transport is working in connection with the bill now before the house is not to attempt to create a condition which will1 deceive the Canadian people into thinking they have not put into this railway the money which has been put into it, but rather to clarify the present position in that regard' and to maintain before the Canadian people the amount which they have put into the roads as representing what it really is, the equity of the Canadian people in the railway after the fixed securities in the hands of the public have been taken care of. True, the value of that equity, as my right hon. friend says, is represented in the public debt of Canada at this moment. True, the Canadian people are paying the interest on that portion of the public debt just as they are paying it on the rest of the public
