debt, but with this qualification: The portion set up in the balance sheet of the Canadian National Railways to-day, plus the rate of interest calculated upon it, does not represent the cost of that amount of money to-day to the Canadian people. It represents a calculation based upon the rates obtaining when the various loans were made, under the contracts connected with them. As a matter of fact, there is little comfort in looking at our railway balance sheet picture, but there is this much comfort, at any rate, that the amounts set up by way of indebtedness in the present balance sheet do not cost the Canadian people quite as much as the amount set out there, for the reason that as a consequence of lower interest on moneys and refunding operations, the average cost of the public debt has been reduced, while the rates used1 for computation in the balance sheet remain about the same as those existing when the obligations were undertaken in the first place. To-night we have listened to a profitable discussion. The contribution made by the leader of the opposition in bringing to our attention the manner in which post offices are run in New Zealand and Australia should prompt the committee to inquire into ways and means of operating this great public utility on a more businesslike basis. I have not been a member of the house for very long, but during my short stay I have had all kinds of persons speak to me regarding the manner in which rural mail contracts and post office appointments are undertaken and made. As I am a non-government
member, of course that does not mean that one has been approached for such appointments, but it does mean that in Canada, to a great extent apparently, the post office is looked upon as an arm for political patronage.
It seems to me that in all probability many of our troubles in the Post Office Department proceed from that particular cause. Where you have that kind of appointment and' that kind of operation I believe you have inefficiency. As one who a few years ago had to make some investigation of the civil services of both New Zealand and Australia, I know that the efficiency of their services is due largely to the fact that they have been removed from political patronage. The sooner hon. members face the matter squarely and realize that we shall never have our post office or any other institution efficient until we remove political patronage from the service, the sooner shall we have the service for the benefit and use of the people of Canada.
Is it not efficient now?

No, it is not. The fact that we had the statement brought down in the way in which it has been brought down in the last two years proves that we know nothing about the service in detail. The discussion we have had to-night regarding subsidies and payments for the carrying of mail shows that so far as we are concerned we have no conception of the business basis of the Post Office Department. When an organization such as that department cannot produce before the House of Commons a statement giving us a more approximate idea of the relative costs of the various services, and the relative receipts, such department is not efficient.

The hon. member
attributes it to politics?
To a very large degree I attribute it to political patronage within the service.

Mr. ISNOR; 

when he speaks of the inefficiency of employees of the department. I come in close touch with the Post Office Department in Halifax, the centre for Nova Scotia, and! I want to say that we have an exceptionally efficient and loyal staff. I believe the same condition applies equally throughout the whole province.
May I point out that we of the province of Nova Scotia appreciate the air mail service given in New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, but unfortunately that service has not yet reached Nova Scotia. Ours is still the only province in Canada which is not served by air mail. May I draw particularly to the attention of the minister the fact that I believe we are entitled to the service, along regular lines. However, at this time the department has received from one of the air mail lines an offer under which it will not cost Canada a single cent to provide air mail service to Nova Scotia. With an offer such as that before it, I fail to understand why the government has not accepted the service and put it into operation in Nova Scotia. I draw the matter to the attention of the Postmaster General in the hope that he will not lose much time in giving air mail service to our province.

May I make a correction, because I do not wish to be misunderstood. I was not criticizing the efficiency of the permanent employees under the civil service commission, but was discussing more particularly the service in the rural areas and the patronage to steamship and railway lines. I was not referring to the general, permanent service.
Mr. BOTHWELL; What particular complaint has the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar about the rural service, and where does he believe the Post Office Department loses money through any patronage he might have seen exercised in his district?

Mr. COLDWrELL: I am pleased to answer that question. I would say that efficient people carrying the mail and running the post offices are changed sometimes when there are changes of government. It requires a considerable amount of time for a man or a woman to become efficient in a new job. Every time there is a change a new official must be trained, and I say that is a source of inefficiency. It lowers the morale of the whole service.

I can speak only of conditions as I know them, and I must say that I am not very favourably impressed by some of the work that has been done by the civil service commission. In the constituency which I have the honour to represent I know of instances where men have been appointed by the civil service commission to jobs for which they were in no way qualified. I know of one man who obtained marks of 98 per cent in the examination and yet was passed by in favour of a man who knew practically nothing about the work to be done. That is aside from the Post Office Department. I have represented my constituency since 1925 and during that time there have been only two changes in postmasters. These changes were not made because of political patronage. One man was using the post office as a recruiting ground for a political party, and when the citizens of the district protested he refused to desist. Such a man was not fitted for the post he held and he was dismissed. If that could be called political patronage, then there was political patronage. After looking over the situation for many years in my constituency, I have not seen any inefficiency. I do not believe the charge made by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar is correct, unless the situation in other parts of the country is different from that which I have observed in mine.

I should like to say a word or two on behalf of the rural mail carriers. These carriers do not come under the civil service; they are not appointed through patronage, which might perhaps be better; they carry on under the tender system. There are men in this country carrying the mails for less than the service is worth. They also have to make a considerable capital investment to provide motor cars. These people should be protected even against themselves. I should like to see the Postmaster General (Mr. Elliott) give some consideration to these rural mail carriers.
Another point to which I should like to refer is the order in council which stipulates that twenty per cent of the permanent staff

must be temporary. This places a great hardship on many postal employees. Some of them must work ten, fifteen or twenty years before they are placed on the permanent staff. During those years they are precluded from contributing to the superannuation fund. I ask the Postmaster General if something cannot be done to permit men who have been postmen for, say three, four, five or six years to be placed on the permanent staff and not to allow them to go into old age while still on the temporary list.

As a new member I was
surprised that I did not have to pay any postage on the letters I posted. If the Postmaster General and his staff did not do anything but carry the letters of the 245 members of this house, they would certainly be deserving of commendation. A dollar a day for 245 members-the hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deachman) is not here-for 100 days, which would be a short session, would mount up into the millions.
No.
I am not a mathematician.
Hear, hear.

I want to say that I am better able to pay my postage now than I was before I came into the house. I think members of parliament should pay their own postage and thus put the post office on a paying basis. I have just one criticism to make. I should like to see the letter carriers get their holidays on Christmas day and Good Friday.

I have been trying for some time to get around to answering my hon. friend, but there seems to be so much zeal in offering commendation of the present system that I have not had an opportunity. With regard to Nova Scotia, I may say to my hon. friend that it will be a great pleasure to the officials of the department and myself when we reach the time when we can give the service to *which he has just referred. I may say that this matter is receiving serious consideration and I hope to be able to make some reply before very long.
With regard to the hon. member who spoke last (Mr. Mclvor), I want to say that he stands in a class by himself. I have been in this house for a good many years and his is the first protest I have ever heard against the franking privilege granted to members of the house.
His mail must be light.

Perhaps I
could answer two or three of my hon. friends who have spoken. As far as Christmas day and New Year's day are concerned, I do not see how it would be humanly possible to do without a service on those holidays. If I recall rightly, the receipts for the month of December were a little over $403,000 more than they were a year ago. Indications very early in the season were that this was going to be an unparalleled Christmas season. Apparently this was some indication of how the people of this country felt toward one another. May I refer to the city of Toronto-I do not want to pick out any particular place because I have not always picked out Toronto-
It is a good Tory town.

-as the city *that has sent the best representatives to parliament. However, it has been improving in this connection. Perhaps my hon. friend will sympathize with the officials of the department when I tell him that on one day just preceding the Christmas rush 5,000,000, less 1.000, pieces of mail, incoming and outgoing, were handled in Toronto alone. I should like to say a word with regard to what happens when Christmas day or some other holiday follows a Sunday and a rush is on. I had better explain this, though perhaps I am trespassing on the time of my colleague who is to follow me. We were having Christmas day and other holidays following Sundays. In the large cities, if delivery is not made on Saturday afternoon, the mail that comes in after seven or eight o'clock on Saturday morning stands over until Monday. This year the mail received in the large cities on the day before Christmas and on Christmas day was substantially larger than in previous years. It must not be forgotten that formerly there were deliveries on Christmas day, New Year's day, and all these holidays, and now we are giving to those who handle the mail time off for the hours they serve on the holidays which have been granted them from time to time.

I wished to know whether
the minister had had any protest from postal employees in the various cities. I am sure there have been protests from Vancouver.

Yes, we have had protests. I doubt whether my hon. friend was listening to what I was saying. I said we had a large delegation from the trades and labour council, voicing their grievances and asking for certain changes which they thought should be made, and there was not a mention by any one of them of this matter of mail service on holidays. There have been deputations, but I might mention that this arrangement was arrived at only after serious consultation with representatives of the mail service from one end of Canada to the other.
What would have been the position if the change had not been made? We would have had people carrying, on the morning after Christmas, much more mail without any additional pay. We are now paying them extra. It is our intention to ask for an additional sum of about $185,000 to pay for deliveries on holidays and for the time, between now and March. 1, that it will take to work off that over-time. It was thought that that work should be done to a large extent by people who are without jobs, and that the working off of the over-time should proceed during what is, to unemployed men, the hardest period of the year, namely between December 15 and April 1. I am assured by some of those who are affected that it has been a veritable godsend to them to have that extra work at Christmas and to have the prospect of additional work in the first three or four months of this year.

With regard to Christmas
work, one postman told me he was grateful to be able to deliver on Christmas day because he received in Christmas boxes twice the amount he had ever received before.

There is no
question about that. You can always get an agitation; they are much easier to start than to stop. But I may say there is no serious agitation against this arrangement. In certain sections serious objections on religious grounds have been made, but we have throughout this country a pretty good class of postmasters, exercising a wise discretion,, and except in the larger places, where the mail can be delivered by midnight on Christmas eve, there is no great amount of pressure exercised for more than one delivery on Christmas day. We want to accord to those

who object on religious grounds the greatest privileges possible, but I would say to them- and I know they are conscientious-that in the households of many of them they have maids working who are doing much more work on Christmas day than they do on any other day of the year. The same applies to New Year's day. Then there are the telegraphers from, one end of the country to the other who work competitively in sending out messages at Christmas, which necessitates much heavier work on Christmas day than on any other day of the year. The same applies to those engaged in work on the street railways, the trains, and various other services. All we are trying to do is, in view of the necessities of the time, to have the mail delivered in an orderly way. Take the city of Montreal: with the immense amount of mail received there this year, if there had not been a delivery on Christmas day the Christmas mail would not have been all out by the following Saturday.
How was it done in previous years?

It was done,
until a few years ago, in exactly the same way as we are doing it now. Then they got New Year's day, and later on, Christmas day, and may I inform the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Heaps) that what was said by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Baker) is absolutely true-the great majority of these postal carriers get much better treatment if they deliver their mail on Christmas day than if they wait until the day after. Also, Christmas cards this year were much more numerous than they ever were before in the history of the department. That, I think, is a hopeful sign of the times.

to the rural mail carriers, first of all it would be necessary to change the act. By section 67, contracts for the transportation of mail, if the amount is over $200, must be advertised for a certain length of time and then let to the lowest competent tenderer who furnishes proper sureties. There is nothing new about the tender system. What would my hon. friend say if, when we were letting a contract, for instance, for one of these buildings, it was not accepted because somebody bid too low? When I was Minister of Public Works a number of people bid so low they failed. The confederation block is an example. The receiver went on and completed it. These people tender at a certain price. Their tenders are not known to anybody else, and the man who tenders at a particular price knows he would rather have that job at that price than not have it. Let me give an example of what happened in one of the rural routes out here. Where we used to have, a few years ago, six or eight tenders on a rural route we had forty-two tenders. I would not be sure about this, but I believe I had a representative from every one of the forty-two, the highest of which was more than double the lowest, wanting the contract at the lowest tender. These people are driving out through the country serving people who are working perhaps longer hours at harder work for the same amount of money they are getting, and I know of very few mail carriers who want to throw up their job at the present time. I should like to see them get more; they will get more as times improve, and I believe we have definite evidence that times are improving. I know, having made that statement, it will render unnecessary any explanation to the hon. member for Parkdale.

I shall not refer to the matter the minister last spoke about, but I want to refer to something he said in reference to Toronto in connection with engaging a large number of temporary posties to permit the regular posties having a few days off after Christmas in compensation for having worked all Christmas day. A postie called at my neighbour's house shortly after Christmas andi as he was a stranger to the community he was asked where he came from. It turned out that he did not belong to Toronto but came from one of the Yorks. I happened to accost him a day or two afterwards and I learned that >he had a temporary job-I suppose a job such as the minister has referred to-and I understand that it will last perhaps until the first of March. I would not for a moment charge the minister with being
partisan. I know he is far too broad-minded to issue orders that all these extra postal employees should belong to the Liberal party. He would1 not do anything like that.
I am glad to hear the hon. member say that.

I like the broad view he takes of these matters and I know that if he had his way, when these poor unfortunates wanted jobs, he would issue an order to the authorities in Toronto to engage men just as they came along without regard to their politics. But I made inquiries myself, and with respect to all those about whom I inquired I found that back to their great-grandmothers 

at any rate as far back as the inquisitor could go-they were supporters of the Liberal party. I know the minister does not want anything like that, and I should greatly appreciate it if he would instruct the authorities in Toronto it is his wish that in the selection of these temporary employees no questions should be asked concerning their politics. I should like him to issue a warning to the Liberal association there not to send letters to these applicants requiring them to have cards of the Liberal association. Let him warn the officials in Toronto it is his wish that anybody, Jew or Gentile, Hottentot or Greek, Grit or Tory, or anybody else, shall be equally welcome to be engaged by the department.
I think my hon. friend knows the standing of the postmaster in Toronto in charge of the work there.
A very capable man.

One of the most capable men who can be found in any service, and that applies to most of the employees throughout the whole postal service, notwithstanding what some of my hon. friends have said to-night. His instructions were to get the best men who could be obtained for this work, and from what my hon. friend says, I gather that he succeeded.

I want to ask the minister, in view of his avowed intention of giving us a more simplified statement, whether he would recommend a change in the present practice of using postage stamps on cheques. I have raised this question because if the excise stamp were used, the proceeds would go into the consolidated revenue fund and in that event I believe the Post Office Department might show a deficit rather than a profit.

It is amusing to hear the Postmaster General in his present vein of talk, and I wish to congratulate him upon the

amount of information he has brought to the house. He has brought down more than any Postmaster General has done since I have been a member. No doubt this is due to the questions put last year which he has endeavoured to answer to-night. There is no general complaint at all about the Postmaster General or about the personnel of the Post Office Department, because our Canadian postmen cannot be excelled. But the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) mentioned something which is no doubt true, that politics was played to some extent at Christmas and has been since then. It was intimated that 200 letter carriers were required and an examination was held for the purpose of establishing an eligible list in Toronto; yet, from that day to this, that eligible list has been filled through hon. members who sit in this house, representing North York and one of the Torontos. They can go to the postmaster with three or four names of persons and they are appointed. Then people say to me, " My goodness! Have you lost all your prestige?" I reply, "I have nothing to say just now; go to my friends or to the defeated candidate; he may help you to get an appointment." We never played that game in Toronto until this Christmas. I was closely associated with the Post Office Department and the Public Works Department as the minister knows, and I can assure the committee we never played politics. The work was divided among the different ridings and the returned soldiers got their share. The thing was fair. This year, however, it was an absolute racket, and I am sorry to say the returned men received little consideration. The hon. member for York North (Mr. Mulock) and the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Factor) were the ones who filled every job they could find in the post office. I am glad to say, however, that our party never played a game of that kind, because we divided the work.
We have heard a great deal to-night about estimates, gross receipts and so on, but at no time have I ever found a Postmaster General able to tell us anything beyond gross receipts; he never knew the expenditures. To-night we have received some information, but I do not think we have yet had sufficient to satisfy this committee that the Postmaster General or anyone connected with the department is running it efficiently. This is due largely to the fact that the Public Works department and the Department of Trade and Commerce do not keep track of the services they render to the post office, the cost of carrying mails on the ships, and the cost of buildings supplied by the Department of Public Works. I do not like to interrupt the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Spence) but I cannot help thinking how interesting it is to find my hon. friends to my right objecting so strongly to patronage. It appears to me that there is always an objection to patronage on the part of hon. members in that section to the left of the Speaker.
I do not object; I say there should be a limit.

The hon. member's objection is not to patronage in principle but to the way it is carried on. In fact, if patronage were confined to the constituency of the hon. member it would not be so bad, but it is when someone from outside intervenes that patronage is bad, in whatever way it is carried on. I think the present Postmaster General has been good in comparison with his predecessors, but I wish he could eliminate patronage entirely. It would save him a great deal of trouble if he did. The number of jobs given by a member at Christmas time may amount to a dozen or a hundred as the case may be. If the opportunity were given to me of handing out patronage I would not want to take it. I do not think it is right that any member of this house should exercise patronage at all. The hiring of employees should be left entirely to the discretion of the officials of the various departments of the government, and members of parliament of whatever stripe should not interfere. After all, we expect these departments of the government to be run efficiently, and there cannot be efficiency if members of parliament keep interfering with the administration. The best thing that could happen, from the standpoint both of members of parliament and of efficiency of administration, would be for the officials of the departments themselves to have complete control of the men and women employed under them. I know the condition complained of has existed for a number of years. I believe the Post Office Department during the regime of the present Postmaster General has been freer from this fault than in former years.

Not in Toronto.

Toronto has always been a bad spot. Possibly, if the members from Toronto would get together and appeal to the Postmaster General, he might see that the abuses which apparently were prevalent during the last period when temporary employees were hired, dio not occur again. To-night I would appeal to the Postmaster General to see to it that in future years, when extra help is required for the postal service of this country during the Christmas rush, help is hired from the regular employment agencies or other agencies of a similar kind.
Or from the available list.

Or from the available list if that is the desire. It is most unfair, if what has been pointed out is true, that at the behest of a department of the government men should prepare for examinations; that they should write those examinations and perhaps be first on the eligible list, and then that a member of parliament should come along and practically eliminate the list, by employing a few preferred individuals instead of the men who happen to be on the list. I do not think anything could be more unfair than that. There is nothing that brings parliament or a member of parliament into greater disrepute than things of that sort. We would all be better off if we could eliminate patronage from our activities and give our jobs to the most efficient men available for the kind of work that is to be performed.
If I may say a word further, Mr. Chairman, the situation of the postal workers has been discussed this evening. On behalf of our Canadian postal workers I wish to say this:
I think they are an efficient set of public employees, and further I believe that they are prepared to cooperate and assist to the full in an endeavour to make of the Post Office Department an efficient public utility. That being so, I think the way the postal employees were handled by the government or by the officers of the Post Office Department just prior to the Christmas rush was most unfair and, I would add, most unfortunate. It was a bad thing. It is wrong in principle to take away from the employees the holidays they have enjoyed for so many years. The fact that maids may work on Christmas day, that the telegraph companies may operate, that trains may run, that street railway lines may operate, does not in any way excuse the Post Office Department for compelling these postal workers to deliver mail on Christmas day. There is no analogy between the postal service and, say the operation of a street railway system, for the 
simple reason that a transportation system is essential, and it is necessary that it operate every day of the week. On the other hand, it is not so essential that mail be delivered twice on Christmas day, for the very obvious reason that when a postal worker takes mail to a business section on that day he finds practically all the stores and offices closed'. I believe it was the experience of many men delivering mail on Christmas day that they had to take back to the post office a great deal of the mail; at least that is what I have been told by some of t.he employees who were delivering mail on that day. So I say there is no analogy. If, as the Postmaster General claims, it is wrong for maids to be working and wrong for other services to operate on Christmas day, I do not see how he can argue that two wrongs make a right, and really that is what his argument amounts to.
More than that, however, I object to what was done because I believe there was an important principle involved. It is this:	I believe this government is in favour of the principle of collective bargaining; at least I hope so. It has been stated many times by hon. gentlemen opposite that they are in favour of that principle. It is against the principle of collective bargaining between employee and employer for the government, as the employer in this case, to lay down a set of rules and say to the employees, who have had no opportunity of discussing the rules with their employers, "You have to abide by these rules whether you like it or not." That is really what happened in regard to the change of hours.

May I just
correct my hon. friend. Before the details were arranged, the first question asked was, "Are w,e going to be paid for this overtime?" They discussed the matter with the officials of the department, principally with Mr. Underwood who is in charge of that branch, and while they would have preferred cash for the overtime, I think the great majority of them were fair enough to see that they, having jobs already, should be satisfied that somebody who was without a job should get paid for that extra time. That was what took place.

May I ask the Postmaster
General if this arrangement, this change in the hours and conditions of labour, was taken up by the officials of the department with the unions concerned?

I do not
know about the unions; I know that before the details were settled the postal employees met with the officials of the department. I

Supply-Post Office
do not know whether they suggested the interview or whether the department suggested it, but they were here and the discussion as to working out the details lasted a whole day.
Can the Postmaster General inform the committee as to who were here?

I think I
have the names, but I could not give them offhand.

I do not want to know the
names of the individuals, but I should like to know whom they represented. I have not the information before me; it is up in my room, but I am told that the men themselves were not consulted as to these changes. So far as they were concerned, there were notices posted in the various post offices, and they had to abide by these new regulations. I feel that our government, as an employer of labour, should be a model employer. When the government makes changes which may arouse resentment among those affected, such changes should not be brought about until the men themselves have been consulted so that a more amicable adjustment may be arrived at between the government and the men concerned. The Postmaster General and the officials of the department may have different information, but I am told that this was not done in this instance. I know that in Winnipeg a mass meeting was held and a good deal of objection was expressed to the new regulations which were put into effect by the Post Office Department. I know from the expressions of opinion at that meeting that practically all those attending certainly would have liked to have Christmas day off instead of being compelled to take out two loads of mail on that day.

The hon. member for
Winnipeg North (Mr. Heaps) did not speak as a vulgar politician. He spoke as a statesman, and a statesman has no time to receive his electors. He is so busy studying the important problems which may affect the nation that he cannot do anything for the poor little fellow who would like to have a post office in his range or his township just for the convenience of the people around him, the twenty, thirty or forty families who would like to have a post office for their greater convenience. I cannot picture one of those men passing an examination set by a civil service commission which does not know anything about local conditions. Everything is left to the wisdom of the Postmaster General and the officials of his department, who decide first whether it is in the public interest to
establish a post office there, and later whether this one or that one should be appointed postmaster.
My hon. friend does not know about the funny ways of some Tories. I know them better than he does. It is not my custom to trouble anyone in regard to a post office provided that the Tory incumbent does not boast of the fact that he stays there when a Liberal has not a job. The hon. member does not know about all the conditions in the country. He thinks he does, but in fact he does not. He represents a constituency in a very large city, but if he represented a rural constituency in Ontario, Quebec or even Manitoba he would possibly have one of his strongest opponents acting as postmaster in that small locality. That Tory would say, "I am here and I defy the member to dislodge me." That causes some trouble. The member must receive complaints from here and there saying, "That fellow should keep quiet; he has a government job, and he should do his work as postmaster. He should not provoke people. He should not go from house to house canvassing and saying 'I am against him. I have my job and he cannot dislodge me'". That is pretty brassy, and when it is done to the knowledge of the member, the only action left for him, in order not to create trouble for a Tory but to have peace in the community, is to write the Postmaster General and say that within his knowledge so-and-so is creating disturbances by canvassing openly, despite his government job.
That is one point. May I tell the hon. member that I do not believe in the merit system of the civil service commission. He does believe in it, because he does not know about it. I have before me an advertisement for the position of supervisor of time service, and micro-analyst. If anyone approached the hon. member in connection with that job he would say, "I have nothing to do with that; go to the civil service commission." Well, some supporters of the hon. member may admire him for his statesmanlike speeches, but at some time or another they may want a little chance somewhere. We Liberals and Conservatives understand that very well. We try to favour our friends to the greatest extent. We are just vulgar politicians, but the hon. member is a statesman and he will say to that particular man, "Joe"-or Abie or Enoch, as the case may be-"I have nothing to do with that job. You must go to the civil service commission and enjoy the fruits of the merit system. You must fill out your application for the examination, and then if you are the best competitor you will

Supply-Post Office

get the job, under the merit system. I have nothing to do with it." Then my hon. friend makes a wonderful speech about the League of Nations, hours of work or something like that, and does not give anything to anyone.
I cannot understand why the hon. member is elected; it is contrary to human nature.
I might repay the compliment to my hon. friend.

I cannot understand.
Everyone who supports the hon. member may accept his views, support his ideas and believe in his speeches, but on the other hand it is human nature to expect something in return. Hon. members opposite, good Conservatives, understand that very well. I see some who have taken part in provincial politics, and the same condition obtains there. You try to reward your friends the best way you can; it is legitimate.
"To the victor belong the spoils."

Not so much as that; my hon. friend is all wrong when he says that. I do not believe every postmaster should be fired at each change of government. My idea is that two Tories should be fired for every Liberal who was fired by the previous Postmaster General.

You started it.
Mr. PO'ULIOT: One must be honest about this. Afterwards the other Tories keep quiet and remain in their jobs. But when someone is troublesome or is a source of disturbance in the community he should see the long hand of justice, the long hand of the Postmaster General, reaching out to him and talcing his post office from him.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North is a child, if he believes in the merit system. He knows very well that one of the officials of the civil service commission is still in gaol because he was selling jobs. He must know that, because it was in all the papers.
The Prime Minister believes in the merit system too.

He is all wrong in that. He knows one poor fellow is in gaol now because he was selling jobs. The hon. member must know very well that there is more narrow patronage in the civil service commission than there is in any department of the government. The hon. member must know, too, that there is a clique here in Ottawa of ten or twelve-
I rise to a point of order. Are we discussing the department of the minister, or the civil service commission?

I should like to see the hon. member for Eglinton running against the hon. member for Winnipeg North. But to summarize all I have said: I hope some day I may have a private conversation with the hon. member for Winnipeg North, at which time I shall show him my post office files. I have nothing to hide from him or from anybody else. I shall show him human nature at its best and at its worst. Then he must judge for himself, and he will know more about the matter than to-night he has shown he does.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?
Carried.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Item 275.
Post Office-Outside Service

Salaries and allowances, $16,713,338.50.
Mail services, including mail services by air, $14,520,000.	_
Miscellaneous, including $5,000 to provide for payment of compassionate allowances to employees injured while in the performance of their duties or to other persons injured while performing duties in any way connected^ with the postal service or in protecting His Majesty's mails, or to the dependents of such employees or other persons who may be killed while so engaged, payments to be made only on the specific authority of the governor in council, $1,004,600.

Before the item is carried may I say that while I hesitate to impose on the good nature of our friends on the government side of the house at this late hour, I believe that this question of a postal service on Saturday afternoons and statutory holidays is far more important than they realize. Certainly that is true in the cities, and I can speak particularly of Vancouver.
After all, there are thousands of postal employees across Canada who are affected by this new provision. These men are serving Canada, just as we are serving Canada, and I suggest that their position should receive a little more serious consideration than it has to-night. I know hon. members have not meant to consider the matter lightly, but for example there has been talk about Christmas postcards having to be delivered, as though that were the matter of importance.
I believe the issue goes deeper than that. As I understand it the change was made on December 5 of last year, and it was made by order in council or by departmental regulation. I believe, too, that very little warning or notice was given to the postal service. I understand the post offices were given no chance to prepare for the Saturday afternoon and holiday services. In normal times the staff in Vancouver is short, even without the extra work which was added. No previous

Supply-Post Office
provision was made by the department for increasing the staff. In other words, there was no reasonable or common sense arrangement made to increase the staff to a point where it could handle the extra work.
We find that through the order there is to be a full postal service on Saturday afternoons when practically all business offices are closed. In my own office it is a nuisance to have mail delivered on Saturday afternoon, because it is apt to lie around on the floor or be misplaced by the janitor. I am sure the same observation would apply to thousands of offices across Canada.
Then, in addition there is to be a full- not a partial-postal service in post offices. I assume that service will be given on New Year's day, Good Friday, Victoria day, July 1) Labour day, Thanksgiving day, Remembrance day and Christmas day. On almost all these holidays not only offices but also all stores are closed. Surely there is no need for mail delivery on these statutory holidays. I suggest that there has been no great demand from the general public for mail delivery on these holidays. I understand that postal employees have had their Saturday afternoons and other holidays for many years, so why should a change be made at this time? There is no such thing as overtime pay; a man simply works more one week and less the next. It is all rather uncertain; he does not know what days he will have off. I know there has been the greatest confusion in Vancouver as to when the men will have their time off, and I am sure similar confusion must have arisen in other large post offices.
Will this affect the mail collection service? I understand that contracts for the collection of mail are largely on a six-day basis. Are we to have full mail collections on all holidays and on Saturday afternoons? The minister has said that the extra cost of providing this holiday service will be nearly $200,000. The extra staff required is not being obtained through the civil service commission. In Vancouver the same complaint is made that was made in Toronto. I know that many war veterans were unable to obtain the temporary work simply because they were not of the right stripe politically. It is all very confusing for the service. I understand there has been no request from the public generally for this service. There may have been requests from a few business firms, but I believe that is all. In fact, I understand that the public were more or less surprised when this service was inaugurated.
The Postmaster General has mentioned the difficulty when a holiday falls on a Monday.
Surely it would be possible to make special arrangements to handle the mail on these occasions. I suggest that this change is not fair to the postal employees of Canada and that the matter should be given further consideration. It is a step backwards. In British Columbia the weekly half holiday and statutory holidays are provided for by a provincial statute, but here we have dominion civil servants being obliged to work when other employees, with very few exceptions, have the holidays. I think it is unnecessarily disturbing the postal service and I ask the minister to give the matter serious consideration. I believe he would alleviate the condition if he realized how much dissatisfaction has been caused.
What item are we on?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Item 275.
What about item 16?

That was
carried the first of the evening.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In order to clarify the
situation might I point out that the committee has been discussing item 275. For almost the last two hours the matters discussed would fall within the limits of item 16.

Earlier in the evening
I said that the minister was allowing a lot of discussion which was entirely irrelevant. Item 16 is the only item I have heard of to-night.

That was carried earlier in the day. The leader of the opposition mentioned that it had been called "carried" the last time the post office estimates were under discussion, but had not been marked as such.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I may say to the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) and to the other members of the committee that item 16 was carried. I then called item 275.
I never heard it.
I never heard it until this moment.
I do not think anyone here heard the word "carried" in connection with item 16, and we certainly never heard item 275 called.
Surely you do not expect to carry an item of over a million like that.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Item 275 is before the committee; item 16 was carried.

I did not agree to item 16 carrying.

Supply-Post Office
I spoke before that item was declared carried.

I may say to the committee that I have been following things pretty closely. I am sure if the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) were here, he would bear me out when I say that it was carried and marked "carried." We then proceeded to item 275, which contains many items that were partly discussed the other evening.
Item 275 has not been called to-night so far as I remember.
Is it possible for me to have an answer to my question?

I must apologize to my hon. friend, but I have been trying to answer his question. I understand his question was with regard to the stamps issued by the Department of Finance for use on cheques and as to whether some method could be devised whereby postage stamps would be used entirely for that purpose. The stamps issued by the Department of Finance are excise stamps, and I suppose that is why they were issued. However, a large number of postage stamps are used on cheques. There is no way I know of, without incurring an expense out of proportion to the value of the information obtained, by which we would be able to check up how many excise stamps and how many postage stamps are used on cheques.

I do not think the minister understood my question clearly, but I can understand that as there was considerable confusion in the committee. The minister has intimated his intention of giving us a more simple statement and I was asking if he would recommend the use of excise stamps only on cheques, and abolish the practice of using postage stamps. I have made an inquiry at various banks throughout the country and I understand that stamps used on cheques run about forty per cent postage stamps. I understand the revenue derived from the sale of excise stamps goes into the consolidated revenue fund, while that derived from the sale of postage stamps goes into the Post Office Department. When I see an item of $27,000,000 for stamps with a surplus of one and three quarter millions, it might well be that the department could show a deficit rather than a profit. I would suggest that either post office stamps or excise stamps be used exclusively.

I understand for a time it was not permissible to use postage stamps on cheques, but many complaints were made, particularly in the rural
[The Chairman.]
districts, as to the difficulty in obtaining excise stamps. I think the preponderance of public opinion is in favour of the system as it now exists. I shall be glad to discuss with the Minister of Finance as to whether it is possible to make some arrangement which will clarify the situation as to the revenue derived from each source.
With regard to what has been said by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green), there is always a possibility of making some changes which will be of advantage to both parties. I have not found any lack of cooperation among those who are getting time off for Saturday afternoons and the holiday service that they give, and I think it will be found that they prefer a week's holiday at a time to a half day some Saturday afternoon and odd holidays at other times. I repeat that we shall cooperate with them as far as we can and do the best possible under any circumstances which may arise. We came to the conclusion that we must immediately adopt a system of working on Saturday afternoons and holidays, and we shall make such improvements as we can in agreement with the men engaged in the work.

Is it not possible to work
with skeleton staffs on statutory holidays and on Saturdays?
In the smaller places that is being done.

But is it necessary to have a delivery on statutory holidays? Take any holiday, even Christmas; I think the great majority of our people were accustomed to doing without mail on Christmas day. They would rather have the postman get his day off.

As regards
the suggestion of skeleton staffs, I can agree with my hon. friend to a large extent so far as the offices are concerned, but in view of our experience so far, I cannot agree with him as regards doing away with deliveries on holidays.
But let us take deliveries on, say, July 1. Is there any reason why the ordinary home owner should get mail on July 1?

It seems to me that the only "skeleton" there will be in the mail service will be the rural mail delivery man. He is the one about whom I am concerned. Much time has been taken up in discussion about these postal men working on Christmas day. It is a repetition of the same old thing; anything that emanates from the urban centres must receive a great deal of consideration.

Supply-Post Office
Yet these postal men get pretty good pay; they also receive free suits of clothes, and I do not think they are deserving of nearly as much consideration as those engaged on rural mail delivery.
I have only two minutes, but I want to take this opportunity of supporting the views of the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) with regard to the position our rural mail delivery service is in. We discussed that for a few minutes, but we spent an hour and a half talking about postal service in the cities. In my constituency there is a man who drives the rural mail over a route of twenty-one miles for $445, or $1.40 a day. I appreciate the stand taken by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Heaps) on behalf of labour, but I do not know why there is so much consideration for these people who happen to live in the specially privileged centres. Lots of farmers have to milk cows on Christmas day and hurry around in preparing Christmas dinner, very often for visiting aunts and uncles. There should be a little consideration for the class to which I have referred, and I hope the Postmaster General (Mr. Elliott) will appreciate the situation with which we are faced. It looks as though there is going to be an increase in the cost of living. What will be the position of these rural mail carriers when they find the cost of living has become so high that they cannot maintain themselves? It is not very difficult for some high-salaried men to get bonuses. The city postal service employees, I believe, come under the Civil Service Act and are entitled to superannuation. But the rural mail man is not protected in any way. As soon as he is off his job, well, he is off, and whether or how he lives does not seem to give anybody any concern.
The minister has been extremely kind and has given us a great deal of latitude in discussing his department. I very much appreciate his attitude and have nothing but praise for the manner in which he is conducting his department. I do not think there have been many complaints in regard to political patronage. In my constituency, at least, there has been no evidence of it.
I should like to get a statement from the minister as to what will be done on behalf of these poorly paid rural mail carriers in view of the way the cost of living is going up.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is quite evident that hon. gentlemen are not going to allow an item to pass to-night. That moves me to say something, in moving that the committee rise, which I think should be said in the interests of the conduct of this committee. The misunderstanding which occurred this evening arose entirely out of our having permitted discussion on an item which was not before the committee. Had discussion been confined to item 16, there would not have been in anyone's mind any question as to whether that item had been passed. In spite of that, for practically the whole of this evening, and most of a former evening, during which post office estimates were before the committee, discussion was permitted over the whole range of the Post Office Department, although according to the rules we should have been discussing item 16, which would have restricted the discussion to the subject matter of the item. I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that there is only one way by which to avoid in future misunderstandings of that kind, and that is to hold the discussion strictly to the item under discussion. I believe it would be in the interests of all of us if that were done, and would prevent future misunderstandings. I move that the committee rise,, and report progress and ask leave to sit again.. It is understood that item 16 is carried.
Progress reported.

At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
